title: Defining Deviance
description: What counts as deviance, why it varies, and how crime is socially constructed

concepts.title: Deviance as Normative Violation
concepts.contentHtml:
Sociologists define deviance as behaviour, belief, or condition that violates the norms of a social group. Norms are shared expectations: from manners to mores to codified law. Deviance is therefore not the same as harm or immorality — it is whatever a community treats as a breach of its rules.

This produces three useful distinctions. Folkways are everyday customs whose violation invites mild disapproval (eating with the wrong utensil). Mores carry stronger moral weight (adultery, disrespect for the dead). Laws are mores formalised by the state, with sanctions attached.

Crucially, deviance is relational: an act is deviant only in relation to a particular audience and context. A behaviour praised in a war zone — taking life — may be punished in peacetime. Sociology brackets the question of whether the act is 'really' wrong and asks instead: who treats it as wrong, and with what consequences?

concepts.title: Cultural and Historical Relativity
concepts.contentHtml:
What counts as deviant varies dramatically across time and place. Tattoos signalled criminality in 1950s America and now appear on schoolteachers. Homosexuality was a felony in most US states before 1962 and is now constitutionally protected. Cannabis was a folk medicine, then a federal crime, and is again a regulated commodity in much of the country.

This relativity is not the same as the philosophical claim that nothing is really wrong. It is an empirical observation about which acts get classified as wrong by which authorities. Howard Becker's slogan: 'Deviance is not a quality of the act the person commits, but rather a consequence of the application by others of rules and sanctions to an offender.'

Sociologists therefore study not just rule-breakers but rule-makers — the moral entrepreneurs, legislators, journalists, and professionals who define which behaviours warrant control, and against whom enforcement is concentrated.

concepts.title: The Social Construction of Crime
concepts.contentHtml:
Crime is the legal subset of deviance: acts the state has criminalised. But which acts those are is itself a social and political achievement. Workplace deaths from employer negligence kill more Americans annually than homicide, yet most are handled administratively. Conversely, possession of small amounts of drugs has produced mass incarceration.

The social construction view does not deny that murder, theft, and assault cause real harm. It points out that the boundary between 'crime' and 'civil wrong' or 'tragic accident' is drawn by humans and reflects power: who can be prosecuted, who writes the statutes, who frames the moral panic.

Edwin Sutherland's coinage of white-collar crime in 1939 was a deliberate provocation: corporate price-fixing and securities fraud cause vast aggregate damage but were rarely treated as criminal. The very category of 'crime' had been narrowed to street offences committed by the poor.

title: Durkheim, Anomie, and Strain
description: Why deviance is functional, and how social structure produces it

concepts.title: Durkheim: The Function of Deviance
concepts.contentHtml:
Emile Durkheim argued in The Division of Labor in Society (1893) that deviance is functional for society. By punishing offenders, a community ritually reaffirms its shared values and clarifies the boundary between right and wrong. A society of saints would still find sins to punish, because punishment is what makes solidarity visible.

Deviance also drives social change: yesterday's heretic is tomorrow's reformer. Without people who breach norms, norms cannot evolve. The civil-rights protester, the whistleblower, and the religious dissident are all deviants in their moment.

Durkheim distinguishes two solidarities: mechanical (premodern, rooted in shared belief) and organic (modern, rooted in interdependence and a complex division of labour). The transition between them is rocky — and produces the conditions for anomie.

concepts.title: Anomie and Suicide
concepts.contentHtml:
In Suicide (1897) Durkheim introduced anomie: a condition of normative deregulation in which the moral guardrails of social life have weakened. When economic booms or busts, rapid mobility, or institutional collapse outpace the moral order, individuals lose their sense of what they are entitled to expect. Aspirations become unbounded; frustration follows.

Durkheim's typology of suicide identified four kinds: egoistic (too little integration into groups), altruistic (too much, as in martyrs), anomic (insufficient regulation, as in the newly rich or newly bankrupt), and fatalistic (oppressive over-regulation, as in slavery).

The argument was methodologically revolutionary. Suicide looks like the most private of acts, yet rates are stable for decades and vary systematically with religion, marital status, and the economic cycle. Social facts — patterns external to any individual — exert real causal force.

concepts.title: Merton's Strain Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Merton's 'Social Structure and Anomie' (1938) reworked Durkheim's concept for American conditions. Society offers cultural goals (wealth, status) but distributes institutional means (education, jobs) unequally. The mismatch produces strain.

Merton mapped five adaptations. Conformity accepts both goals and means. Innovation accepts the goals but uses illegitimate means — theft, fraud, drug dealing. Ritualism abandons the goals but clings to the means (the burnt-out clerk). Retreatism rejects both (the dropout). Rebellion rejects both and substitutes new ones (the revolutionary).

Robert Agnew's general strain theory (1992) broadened the picture: strain comes not only from blocked goals but from the loss of valued things and exposure to negative stimuli — abuse, bullying, discrimination. These produce negative emotions, which, absent prosocial coping, lead to delinquency.

title: Learning, Labelling, and Stigma
description: How deviance is taught by peers and produced by reaction

concepts.title: Sutherland's Differential Association
concepts.contentHtml:
Edwin Sutherland's differential association theory (1939) holds that criminal behaviour is learned in the same way any behaviour is — through interaction in intimate groups. There is no criminal gene, no born offender; there is only exposure to definitions favourable to violation of the law.

Sutherland's nine propositions specify the mechanism. Learning includes techniques (how to pick a lock, how to falsify a balance sheet) and motives, drives, and rationalisations (why this is acceptable here). A person becomes delinquent when their definitions favourable to lawbreaking exceed their definitions opposed.

The theory was a deliberate corrective to biological and psychiatric criminology. It also legitimated the study of white-collar crime: the executive who learns price-fixing from colleagues over lunch is using the same social-learning machinery as the apprentice burglar.

concepts.title: Becker and Labelling Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Howard Becker's Outsiders (1963) shifted attention from the deviant act to the process by which it is labelled. 'Social groups create deviance by making the rules whose infraction constitutes deviance, and by applying those rules to particular people and labelling them as outsiders.'

Edwin Lemert distinguished primary deviance — initial rule-breaking that does not yet alter self-concept — from secondary deviance, which arises when the labelled person reorganises identity around the label. The teenager caught shoplifting becomes 'a delinquent,' is treated as one, and develops a delinquent career partly in response to that treatment.

Labelling theory directs attention to the moral career of the deviant and to the institutions — police, courts, schools, psychiatry — that confer labels selectively. Two kids commit the same act; only one is processed. The processing, not the act, determines who becomes a 'criminal.'

concepts.title: Goffman: Stigma and Spoiled Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
Erving Goffman's Stigma (1963) analysed how a discrediting attribute — a criminal record, a visible disability, a marginal sexuality — turns a person from whole into spoiled, in the eyes of others and often in their own.

Goffman distinguished three kinds: abominations of the body, blemishes of individual character (including criminal stigma), and tribal stigmas attached to race, religion, or nation. He also distinguished the discredited, whose stigma is visible, from the discreditable, who must manage information about a hidden mark — the recovering addict, the formerly incarcerated job applicant.

The work illuminated how stigma functions long after formal punishment ends. Devah Pager's audit studies showed a felony record cuts callbacks for entry-level jobs roughly in half — and far more for Black applicants. Labels are sticky in ways that make rehabilitation a structural, not merely psychological, problem.

title: Control, Subcultures, and Conflict
description: What stops most people from deviating, and who decides which deviance counts

concepts.title: Hirschi's Social Control Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Travis Hirschi inverted the usual question. Instead of asking 'why do people deviate?' he asked 'why don't they?' His Causes of Delinquency (1969) argued that conformity requires explanation: people break rules whenever the social bond is weak.

Hirschi identified four elements of the bond. Attachment to others — parents, teachers, peers — gives us reasons to care about their disapproval. Commitment to conventional pursuits (school, work, reputation) means deviance has costs. Involvement in conventional activities consumes time and opportunity. Belief in the legitimacy of social rules makes obedience feel like the right thing.

Later, with Michael Gottfredson, Hirschi proposed a self-control theory (A General Theory of Crime, 1990): low self-control, set early by parenting, explains the propensity to crime across all categories. Sampson and Laub's life-course work added that turning points — marriage, military, a steady job — can rebuild bonds and produce desistance even after long offending careers.

concepts.title: Subcultures and Opportunity
concepts.contentHtml:
If structure produces strain, what do strained communities do? Albert Cohen's Delinquent Boys (1955) argued that working-class boys, judged by middle-class school standards they cannot meet, develop an oppositional subculture that inverts those standards — making toughness, malice, and short-run hedonism markers of status.

Richard Cloward and Lloyd Ohlin (Delinquency and Opportunity, 1960) added that illegitimate opportunities are themselves unequally distributed. Where stable adult criminal networks exist, youth enter criminal subcultures oriented to theft and racket. Where they do not, frustrated youth form conflict subcultures organised around violence, or retreatist subcultures oriented to drug use.

James Q. Wilson and George Kelling's 'Broken Windows' (1982) was a different subcultural argument: visible disorder signals that no one is watching, encouraging further deviance. The policy that grew from it — order-maintenance policing — has been criticised by Bernard Harcourt and others, who argue the empirical evidence is thin and the social costs of aggressive misdemeanour enforcement fall hardest on poor communities of colour.

concepts.title: Conflict Theory and Foucault
concepts.contentHtml:
Conflict theorists ask whose interests the criminal law serves. Richard Quinney's The Social Reality of Crime (1970) treated criminal definitions as instruments of segments of society with the power to shape public policy. Critical criminology extended this through Marxist, feminist, and race-conscious lenses: laws against vagrancy and theft historically protected property; rape law long treated wives as exempt; drug enforcement disproportionately falls on minorities even where use rates are similar.

Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish (1975) traced the shift from spectacular bodily punishment to the modern prison. Power, he argued, was not abolished but refined: the panopticon, the timetable, the case file, the examination produced docile bodies through surveillance and normalisation rather than force. Prisons fail to reduce crime, but they succeed at producing a delinquent class useful to authorities — and at extending disciplinary techniques into schools, hospitals, and workplaces.

Conflict approaches do not require believing all law is mere domination. They do require asking whose deviance is policed and whose is overlooked.

title: Measuring Crime, Punishing It
description: How we count crime, why it fell, and what mass incarceration did

concepts.title: Three Ways to Count Crime
concepts.contentHtml:
How much crime is there? The answer depends on the instrument. Three main sources, all imperfect.

The Uniform Crime Reports (UCR), compiled by the FBI from local police agencies, count offences known to the police. They miss crimes never reported — the dark figure of crime — and reflect changing reporting practices and police priorities. The newer NIBRS system records incident-level detail.

The National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS), run since 1973, asks a representative sample of households whether they have been victimised. It captures unreported crime but excludes homicide, commercial victimisation, and crimes against children under 12.

Self-report studies ask people, usually adolescents, what offences they have committed. They reveal that minor offending is nearly universal and that the demographic gradient in arrests partly reflects differential enforcement, not differential offending. Triangulating across all three sources is essential; relying on any one in isolation is misleading.

concepts.title: The Great American Crime Decline
concepts.contentHtml:
US violent crime peaked around 1991 and then fell roughly in half by the mid-2010s, a drop unanticipated by virtually every criminologist. The decline appeared across regions, demographics, and offence types, and was matched in Canada and parts of Europe.

No single explanation is sufficient. Plausible contributors, weighted differently by different scholars, include: more police and smarter deployment (hot-spots policing, problem-oriented policing); larger prison populations (incapacitation effects, with sharply diminishing returns); the waning of the crack-cocaine market; changing demographics; the removal of lead from gasoline and paint, which lowered childhood neurotoxic exposure; rising real incomes for the poor; better alarms, locks, and immobilisers reducing opportunity; cultural shifts away from public-space loitering toward screens.

The crime decline is a reminder that long-running rates can change fast, that monocausal stories are usually wrong, and that policymakers tend to overweight whichever cause flatters their prior commitments.

concepts.title: Mass Incarceration and Its Purposes
concepts.contentHtml:
Between 1972 and 2008, the US incarcerated population grew roughly five-fold, from about 200,000 to over 1.5 million in state and federal prisons, with another 700,000 in jails. The US now imprisons at five to ten times the rate of comparable democracies. Black men born in the 1970s without a high-school diploma faced a lifetime imprisonment risk above 60 per cent.

Michelle Alexander's The New Jim Crow (2010) argued that the war on drugs functioned as a system of racialised social control, producing a permanent underclass marked by felony stigma, disenfranchisement, and exclusion from housing and employment. Bruce Western and others document the consequences for families and communities.

Punishment is justified by four classical aims, which often pull apart. Deterrence assumes potential offenders weigh costs; the evidence shows certainty of punishment matters more than severity. Incapacitation works mechanically but with steep diminishing returns and large collateral costs. Rehabilitation can work — cognitive-behavioural and education programmes have evidence — but is hard at scale. Retribution answers a moral demand for proportionate desert. Sociology of deviance asks not only which works, but at what cost, on whom, and decided by whom.
